See deleted comments on this thread for a gory example of the interface going astray. I submitted a top level comment, another user replied, then I replied to them, inadvertently including the text of the original comment in it. When I tried to edit it out, things went very badly. There are two problems here:

  1. The text input for editing a comment at any level of the conversation is flush left at the top of the thread, immediately under the edit box for submission of new top-level comments. Choosing to edit a comment doesn't disable submitting a new top level comment. It's very easy to do one instead of the other.

  2. Editing your comment doesn't reload comments, so you have no idea if the edit happened correctly or not. This can (did, in my case) lead to making multiple attempts to edit a comment. These same multiple attempts to edit a comment can erroneously be submitted as new top-level comments (see point 1).

I ended up deleting all my comments in that thread, probably seriously frustrating the person I replied to, rather than risk continually making the thread worse through editing errors. That can't be good. Comment editing needs to disable comment submission, and give a clear picture of what the edit will actually do, so this sort of thing doesn't keep happening.

I can answer this one... It's actually why I quit being a pharmacist and decided to go back to school for a completely unrelated degree...

I was in the US Air Force, working as a pharmacist. As you may know, the AF has Tricare, which means that active duty members, retirees, and dependents of those two groups can get everything and (essentially) anything for free.

This bothered me because, when I was overseas, I was giving antibiotics to people who didn't have clean drinking water, I was giving pain medication to kids who were caught in the fighting, I was helping people... But, when I came back to CONUS, I was giving inhalers to people who wreaked of cigarette smoke, and cholesterol medication to people who'd bring greasy-ass bags of BK to my window... I wasn't helping people anymore. But the straw that broke the camel's back...

One day, I was filling a LARGE prescription for a patient. It was dozens of boxes of different types of insulin (which are nearly $200 per box for some types of insulin), six or seven boxes of syringes and test strips and a glucose meter (presumably because she wore her last one out from testing so much), and 1000 Metformin.

Now, in layman's terms, there's two types of diabetes: the kind that can't really be changed, and the other that can be monitored and controlled (most of the time) with a proper diet and exercise... Metformin only works for the second one...

So, back to the story: I did the math and this woman was getting nearly $10k worth of insulin medication monthly, and I wanted to see her and assess if this was working because... you know... that a lot of fucking money. When she came to pick up her prescriptions, she was in a Rascal, had one leg, and had two dozen Krispy Kreme doughnuts in her basket. She even complained about how many bags worth of prescriptions she had because they were going to crush her doughnuts.

That's when it hit me: If she had to pay for these meds, would she have gone to KK? Would she have been able to afford it? Would she do this to herself... or am I enabling her bad habits?

Was I enabling the smoker to continue smoking? If he couldn't breathe, and he wasn't getting free inhalers, would he keep smoking?

If a patient couldn't get free Triglide or Atrovastatin, would they be more diligent about their cholesterol and diet instead of splurging for BK?

And, if this woman had to spend $10K on diabetic supplies and medication, would she get off her ass before they take her first leg? So, not only did the military pay this woman's extreme monthly medical bill, but they also paid to amputate her leg as well as her constant doctor visits so that a trained medical doctor can monitor her blood sugar and diet so that she doesn't have to.

Mark my words, this will happen more and more as healthcare becomes more and more free. When people feel entitled to their free, $200 bottle of Novolog, they'll stop feeling as if it's their duty to stay healthy. The medical bills will continue to compound, and get worse and worse.

People who get injured from sports most likely won't need repetitive, constant care like this woman.

Ingredients: 2 large yellow onions, two tomatoes, 3 cloves of garlic, 1 lime, cilantro 2 tbs tomato paste, 1 can stewed tomatoes 3 tbs garlic paste, 3 tbs ginger paste, 2 tbs chilli powder, 2 tbs turmeric,4 tbs garam masala, 4 tbs cumin powder, 4 tbs ground coriander 1 stick of butter, 3 oz. heavy cream, 1 cup plain whole fat yoghurt. 2-3 boneless, skinless chicken breasts

Step 1: Chop up chicken breasts and mix into yoghurt. Add 1 tbs chilli powder, 1 tbs turmeric, 2 tbs garam masala, 2 tbs cumin powder, 2 tbs ground coriander, 3 tbs salt, and 2 tbs black pepper. Marinate for 6-8 hours or overnight.

Step 2: Slice the onions thin and cook slowly over low heat in some vegetable oil and 1 tbs butter. Cook for 20-30 mins until they are an even brown. You want the onions to be extremely broken down because we will blend this to create the base for the sauce. Chop up the tomatoes and add them into the mix around the 15-20 min mark. Chop up the garlic very finely and add it in at this point as well.

Step 3: Remove the chicken from the marinade and shake off excess yoghurt. Cook on high heat in vegetable oil until browned and cooked through (around 10 mins). Take the chicken out of the pan and set aside the pan for now.

Step 4: Blend the onion, tomato, and garlic mixture.

Step 5: Oil the pan you cooked the chicken in and put it on medium heat. Add the rest of the spices. Let the spices heat up and release their flavors (for around a minute), but don’t burn them. Add blended mixture to the pan and put on low heat.

Step 6: Add tomato paste and stewed tomatoes. Add butter, heavy cream, garlic paste, and ginger paste. Chop up a handful of cilantro and add into the mix. Let simmer for 10-15 mins. Salt and adjust spices to taste.

Step 7: Serve over basmati rice. Squeeze a little lime on top and garnish with fresh cilantro.
